points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 1: An introduction to microeconomics: the market system, resource allocation and government intervention
points.title: Relative scarcity and opportunity cost
points.detail: Unlimited wants against limited resources, the basic economic questions, and opportunity cost as the value of the next best alternative forgone.

questions.q: Define relative scarcity and explain how it gives rise to opportunity cost.
answer: Relative scarcity is the economic problem that society's wants are unlimited while the resources available to satisfy them are limited.
Because resources are limited, choosing to use them one way means they cannot be used another way.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone when that choice is made, so every economic decision carries one.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 1: An introduction to microeconomics: the market system, resource allocation and government intervention
points.title: The production possibility frontier
points.detail: Points on, inside and outside the frontier; the meaning of a shift in the curve; and the illustration of opportunity cost and unemployed resources.

questions.q: Explain what a point inside the production possibility frontier indicates and what would cause the whole frontier to shift outwards.
answer: A point inside the frontier indicates that resources are not being fully or efficiently employed, so more of both goods could be produced.
An outward shift indicates an increase in the productive capacity of the economy.
This is caused by an increase in the quantity or quality of resources, such as population growth, investment in capital, or improvements in technology and productivity.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 1: An introduction to microeconomics: the market system, resource allocation and government intervention
points.title: Demand and the factors affecting it
points.detail: The law of demand, movement along the curve versus a shift of the curve, and the non-price factors that shift demand.

questions.q: Distinguish between a movement along and a shift of the demand curve, and name three factors that cause a shift.
answer: A movement along the demand curve is caused only by a change in the price of the good itself, and is called a change in quantity demanded.
A shift of the curve is caused by a non-price factor and is called a change in demand.
Factors causing a shift include changes in disposable income, the prices of substitutes and complements, and consumer confidence.
Changes in tastes and preferences, population, and interest rates on credit also shift the curve.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 1: An introduction to microeconomics: the market system, resource allocation and government intervention
points.title: Supply and the factors affecting it
points.detail: The law of supply, the distinction between movement and shift, and the non-price factors including costs of production, technology, climate and government policy.

questions.q: Explain the effect on the supply curve of an increase in the cost of raw materials, and the resulting change in equilibrium.
answer: Higher input costs reduce the profitability of production at every price, so the supply curve shifts to the left.
At the original price a shortage develops, placing upward pressure on price.
The new equilibrium occurs at a higher price and a lower quantity traded.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 1: An introduction to microeconomics: the market system, resource allocation and government intervention
points.title: The price mechanism and equilibrium
points.detail: How shortages and surpluses generate price signals that clear a market, and the role of relative prices in allocating resources between markets.

questions.q: Explain how the price mechanism reallocates resources when consumer demand for a good increases.
answer: An increase in demand creates a shortage at the existing price, so price is bid upwards.
The higher price signals greater profitability to producers, providing an incentive to expand output.
Resources are drawn into this market from less profitable uses elsewhere, since producers can afford to pay more for them.
The market reaches a new equilibrium at a higher price and quantity, and resources have been reallocated towards the good consumers now want more of.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 1: An introduction to microeconomics: the market system, resource allocation and government intervention
points.title: Price elasticity of demand
points.detail: Calculating and interpreting elasticity, the determinants including substitutes, necessity, proportion of income and time, and the effect on total revenue.

questions.q: A firm raises price by 10 per cent and total revenue falls. Explain what this shows about elasticity and name two determinants.
answer: Total revenue falling after a price rise indicates that quantity demanded fell by more than 10 per cent, so demand is price elastic.
The percentage change in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage change in price, giving an elasticity greater than one in absolute value.
A key determinant is the availability of close substitutes, since consumers can switch readily if the good is not distinctive.
Whether the good is a necessity or a luxury, and the proportion of income it represents, also affect elasticity.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 1: An introduction to microeconomics: the market system, resource allocation and government intervention
points.title: Price elasticity of supply
points.detail: The determinants of supply elasticity including spare capacity, the ability to hold stock and the time period considered.

questions.q: Explain why the supply of agricultural produce is usually price inelastic in the short run.
answer: Production requires a growing season, so output cannot be increased quickly in response to a higher price.
Producers have limited ability to store perishable output to release when prices rise.
Supply therefore responds little to price in the short run, though it becomes more elastic over a longer period as planting decisions adjust.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 1: An introduction to microeconomics: the market system, resource allocation and government intervention
points.title: Types of efficiency
points.detail: Allocative, productive, dynamic and intertemporal efficiency, and the contribution of each to living standards.

questions.q: Define allocative and dynamic efficiency and explain how competitive markets promote each.
answer: Allocative efficiency occurs when resources are allocated to produce the combination of goods and services that maximises the satisfaction of society's wants.
Dynamic efficiency is the speed with which resources are reallocated in response to changing conditions, including through innovation.
Competition promotes allocative efficiency because price signals direct resources to where consumers value them most.
It promotes dynamic efficiency because firms must innovate and adapt quickly to survive against rivals.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 1: An introduction to microeconomics: the market system, resource allocation and government intervention
points.title: Public goods
points.detail: Non-excludability and non-rivalry, the free rider problem, and the reason markets under-supply public goods.

questions.q: Explain why a purely private market will under-supply street lighting.
answer: Street lighting is non-excludable, because a provider cannot prevent a person who has not paid from benefiting from it.
It is non-rival, because one person's use does not reduce the amount available to others.
This creates a free rider problem, as consumers have an incentive not to pay while still receiving the benefit.
Private firms cannot generate sufficient revenue and so under-supply or do not supply the good, which is a source of allocative inefficiency and justifies government provision.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 1: An introduction to microeconomics: the market system, resource allocation and government intervention
points.title: Externalities
points.detail: Positive and negative externalities in production and consumption, the divergence of private and social costs and benefits, and the resulting misallocation of resources.

questions.q: Explain how a negative externality in production leads to allocative inefficiency, using pollution as an example.
answer: A negative externality is a cost imposed on a third party not involved in the transaction, such as pollution affecting nearby residents.
The producer bases output decisions on private costs only, which are lower than the true social costs.
Price is therefore too low and output too high relative to the socially optimal level.
Too many resources are allocated to this activity, so allocative efficiency and living standards are reduced.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 1: An introduction to microeconomics: the market system, resource allocation and government intervention
points.title: Asymmetric information and common access resources
points.detail: Market failure arising where one party has better information than the other, and the overuse of resources that are non-excludable but rival.

questions.q: Explain the market failure caused by a common access resource and give an example.
answer: A common access resource is non-excludable but rival, meaning no one can be prevented from using it but each unit consumed reduces what is available to others.
Ocean fish stocks are an example, since no user can be excluded but each catch reduces the stock.
Each user has an incentive to exploit the resource before others do, and no individual bears the full cost of depletion.
The result is overuse and eventual exhaustion, which is allocatively inefficient and damages intertemporal efficiency.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 1: An introduction to microeconomics: the market system, resource allocation and government intervention
points.title: Government intervention in markets
points.detail: Indirect taxes, subsidies, regulations and advertising as responses to market failure, and the mechanism by which each changes behaviour.

questions.q: Explain how an indirect tax on a good with a negative externality improves allocative efficiency.
answer: An indirect tax raises the cost of production, shifting the supply curve to the left.
Price rises and quantity traded falls, moving output closer to the socially optimal level.
The tax internalises the externality by making producers and consumers bear more of the social cost.
Resource allocation therefore more closely reflects true social costs and benefits, improving allocative efficiency.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 1: An introduction to microeconomics: the market system, resource allocation and government intervention
points.title: Unintended consequences of intervention
points.detail: Black markets, reduced international competitiveness, regressive effects and misallocation arising from poorly designed government intervention.

questions.q: Identify two possible unintended consequences of a high indirect tax on tobacco.
answer: A black market may develop, as consumers switch to untaxed illegal supply, reducing government revenue and undermining the policy.
The tax is regressive, taking a larger proportion of income from low income earners, which worsens the distribution of income.
Demand is highly inelastic for addicted consumers, so the reduction in consumption may be much smaller than intended while the financial burden is large.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 2: Domestic macroeconomic goals
points.title: Strong and sustainable economic growth
points.detail: The definition of the goal, measurement by real GDP and the growth rate, and the reasons growth must be both strong and sustainable.

questions.q: Define the goal of strong and sustainable economic growth and explain what 'sustainable' means in this context.
answer: The goal is the highest rate of growth in real GDP consistent with achieving the other economic goals, commonly cited at around 3 per cent per year.
Real GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced, adjusted for inflation.
Sustainable means the rate can be maintained over time without generating unacceptable inflation, an unsustainable current account deficit or environmental degradation.
Growth that is too fast risks capacity constraints and inflation, while growth that is too slow raises unemployment.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 2: Domestic macroeconomic goals
points.title: Low and stable inflation
points.detail: The definition of the goal and the RBA's target band, measurement by the consumer price index, and headline versus underlying inflation.

questions.q: Explain how inflation is measured and why underlying measures are used alongside headline inflation.
answer: Headline inflation is measured by the percentage change in the consumer price index, which tracks the price of a fixed basket of goods and services bought by metropolitan households.
Underlying measures such as the trimmed mean exclude or reduce the weight of items with unusually large price movements.
Volatile items such as fuel and fruit can distort the headline figure in a single quarter without indicating a change in the ongoing trend.
The RBA targets consumer price inflation of 2 to 3 per cent on average over time, and uses underlying measures to judge the trend.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 2: Domestic macroeconomic goals
points.title: Full employment and the NAIRU
points.detail: The goal of full employment, the natural rate of unemployment, the NAIRU, and the measurement of the unemployment rate, participation rate and underemployment.

questions.q: Explain the concept of the NAIRU and why the goal of full employment is not a zero unemployment rate.
answer: The NAIRU is the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment, the lowest rate that can be sustained without generating accelerating inflation.
Even at full employment there is frictional unemployment as people move between jobs, and some structural unemployment as skills adjust.
Pushing unemployment below the NAIRU causes labour shortages, which bid up wages and lead to cost inflation.
Full employment therefore refers to the elimination of cyclical unemployment, not to a zero rate.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 2: Domestic macroeconomic goals
points.title: Measuring the labour force
points.detail: Definitions of employed, unemployed, the labour force and the participation rate, and the limitations of the unemployment rate as an indicator.

questions.q: Explain how the unemployment rate is calculated and two limitations of it as a measure of labour market conditions.
answer: The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people divided by the labour force, expressed as a percentage.
To be counted as unemployed a person must be without work, actively seeking work and available to start.
A limitation is that it excludes discouraged job seekers who have stopped looking, so it understates labour underutilisation.
It also counts a person working one hour a week as employed, so it does not capture underemployment.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 2: Domestic macroeconomic goals
points.title: Aggregate demand and its factors
points.detail: The components of aggregate demand, and the effect of disposable income, interest rates, consumer and business confidence, exchange rates, terms of trade and overseas growth rates.

questions.q: Explain how a fall in consumer confidence and a rise in interest rates each affect aggregate demand.
answer: A fall in consumer confidence makes households more pessimistic about employment and future income, so they defer purchases and increase precautionary saving.
Consumption spending falls, which reduces aggregate demand.
A rise in interest rates increases the cost of borrowing and the return on saving, reducing both consumption of durables and business investment.
Both factors reduce aggregate demand, which slows economic growth and tends to raise unemployment while easing inflationary pressure.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 2: Domestic macroeconomic goals
points.title: Aggregate supply and its factors
points.detail: Productivity growth, costs of production, climate and natural events, exchange rates and government policy as influences on aggregate supply.

questions.q: Explain how an improvement in productivity affects aggregate supply and the achievement of two economic goals.
answer: Higher productivity means more output is produced from the same quantity of inputs, reducing the unit cost of production.
Aggregate supply increases, shifting the curve to the right and expanding productive capacity.
This assists the goal of low inflation, because lower unit costs reduce cost inflationary pressure.
It also assists strong and sustainable growth, because the economy can grow faster without hitting capacity constraints.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 2: Domestic macroeconomic goals
points.title: Demand inflation and cost inflation
points.detail: The distinction between inflation caused by excessive aggregate demand and inflation caused by rising costs of production, and the policy implications of each.

questions.q: Distinguish between demand inflation and cost inflation and explain why the policy response differs.
answer: Demand inflation occurs when aggregate demand grows faster than the economy's capacity to supply, so buyers bid up prices.
Cost inflation occurs when the costs of production rise, such as wages or imported inputs, and producers pass these on as higher prices.
Demand inflation can be addressed by contractionary budgetary or monetary policy that slows spending.
Contractionary policy is less suitable for cost inflation because it reduces output and raises unemployment without addressing the cost cause, so aggregate supply policies are preferred.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 2: Domestic macroeconomic goals
points.title: Effects of the goals on living standards
points.detail: Material and non-material living standards, and the effect of achieving or failing to achieve each domestic goal on both.

questions.q: Distinguish between material and non-material living standards and explain the effect of high unemployment on each.
answer: Material living standards refer to the quantity of goods and services available per person, closely linked to real income per capita.
Non-material living standards refer to the quality of daily life, including health, leisure, environmental quality and social cohesion.
High unemployment reduces material living standards because those without work have lower incomes and less purchasing power.
It reduces non-material living standards through the stress, loss of self-esteem, poorer health outcomes and social problems associated with joblessness.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 2: Domestic macroeconomic goals
points.title: Conflicts and trade-offs between goals
points.detail: The short-run trade-off between low inflation and full employment, and the potential conflict between strong growth and environmental sustainability.

questions.q: Explain the potential conflict between the goals of full employment and low inflation.
answer: Policies that stimulate aggregate demand raise production, so firms hire more workers and unemployment falls.
As unemployment approaches the NAIRU, labour becomes scarce and firms compete for workers by offering higher wages.
Higher wage costs are passed on as higher prices, generating cost inflation, while strong demand simultaneously generates demand inflation.
Achieving very low unemployment in the short run therefore tends to come at the cost of higher inflation, although productivity growth can ease the trade-off.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 2: Domestic macroeconomic goals
points.title: The business cycle
points.detail: Expansion, peak, contraction and trough; the behaviour of growth, inflation and unemployment in each phase; and the meaning of a boom and a recession.

questions.q: Describe what happens to economic growth, inflation and unemployment during a contraction.
answer: Real GDP growth slows and may become negative, with two consecutive quarters of negative growth commonly described as a recession.
Unemployment rises as firms reduce output, cut hours and lay off workers, so cyclical unemployment increases.
Inflationary pressure eases because aggregate demand is weak and firms have spare capacity, so price rises are harder to sustain.
Material living standards fall as incomes and employment decline, and non-material living standards suffer through the stress of job insecurity.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 2: Domestic macroeconomic goals
points.title: Types of unemployment
points.detail: Cyclical, structural, frictional, seasonal and hard-core unemployment, their causes and the different policy responses each requires.

questions.q: Distinguish between cyclical and structural unemployment and explain why each requires a different policy response.
answer: Cyclical unemployment results from a lack of aggregate demand during a downturn, so firms do not need as many workers.
Structural unemployment results from a mismatch between the skills or location of workers and the jobs available, often following technological change or industry decline.
Cyclical unemployment is addressed by expansionary budgetary or monetary policy that raises aggregate demand.
Structural unemployment is not solved by stimulating demand and requires aggregate supply policies such as retraining and relocation assistance.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 2: Domestic macroeconomic goals
points.title: Consequences of inflation
points.detail: Effects on purchasing power, savers and borrowers, international competitiveness, resource allocation and the distribution of income.

questions.q: Explain three consequences of a sustained rate of inflation well above the target band.
answer: Purchasing power falls, so households on fixed incomes such as pensioners can buy less with the same nominal income, reducing material living standards.
Savers lose because the real return on savings falls and may become negative, while borrowers gain because the real value of their debt is eroded.
International competitiveness declines because Australian goods rise in price relative to those of trading partners, reducing exports and worsening the current account.
High and unpredictable inflation also distorts price signals and discourages long-term business investment.

card.title: Consequences of inflation
card.front: Explain three consequences of a sustained rate of inflation well above the target band.
back: Purchasing power falls, so households on fixed incomes such as pensioners can buy less with the same nominal income, reducing material living standards.
Savers lose because the real return on savings falls and may become negative, while borrowers gain because the real value of their debt is eroded.
International competitiveness declines because Australian goods rise in price relative to those of trading partners, reducing exports and worsening the current account.
High and unpredictable inflation also distorts price signals and discourages long-term business investment.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 3: Australia and the international economy
points.title: Globalisation and trade liberalisation
points.detail: The increasing integration of economies through trade, investment and labour flows, and the removal of tariffs, quotas and subsidies.

questions.q: Explain two effects of trade liberalisation on the Australian economy.
answer: Removing tariffs exposes domestic producers to import competition, forcing them to lower costs and innovate, which improves productive and dynamic efficiency.
Consumers gain access to a wider range of goods at lower prices, improving material living standards.
Resources are reallocated towards industries in which Australia has a comparative advantage, raising the overall value of output.
In the short run, workers in import-competing industries may face structural unemployment, requiring retraining and adjustment assistance.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 3: Australia and the international economy
points.title: Exchange rates
points.detail: Appreciation and depreciation, the demand for and supply of the Australian dollar, and the factors that cause each to change.

questions.q: Explain two factors that would cause the Australian dollar to appreciate.
answer: A rise in Australian interest rates relative to overseas rates increases the return on Australian financial assets, raising demand for the dollar.
A rise in the terms of trade or in commodity prices increases export revenue, raising demand for the dollar to pay for Australian exports.
Increased foreign investment in Australia and stronger overseas economic growth also raise demand for the currency.
An appreciation occurs when demand increases relative to supply, raising the price of the dollar in terms of other currencies.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 3: Australia and the international economy
points.title: Effects of exchange rate movements
points.detail: The effect of an appreciation or depreciation on export competitiveness, import prices, inflation, growth and the current account.

questions.q: Explain the effects of a depreciation of the Australian dollar on inflation and on economic growth.
answer: A depreciation raises the price of imports in Australian dollars, directly increasing the cost of imported consumer goods and imported inputs.
This adds to cost inflation, which works against the goal of low and stable inflation.
Exports become cheaper for overseas buyers, so export volumes rise, and imports become relatively expensive, so consumers switch to domestic substitutes.
Net exports therefore increase, raising aggregate demand and supporting economic growth and employment.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 3: Australia and the international economy
points.title: The terms of trade
points.detail: The index of export prices relative to import prices, the causes of movement, and the effect of a rise or fall on national income and the current account.

questions.q: Define the terms of trade and explain the effects of a sustained improvement on the Australian economy.
answer: The terms of trade is the ratio of the index of export prices to the index of import prices, expressed as an index.
An improvement means export prices have risen relative to import prices, so a given volume of exports buys more imports.
Export revenue and national income rise, boosting incomes in the export sector, company profits and tax receipts, which supports growth and the budget position.
An improvement usually also causes the dollar to appreciate, which reduces the competitiveness of other export and import-competing industries.

points.area: Unit 3: Australia’s living standards — AoS 3: Australia and the international economy
points.title: The balance of payments
points.detail: The structure of the current account and the capital and financial account, the meaning of a deficit or surplus, and the relationship between the two accounts.

questions.q: Describe the two main accounts in the balance of payments and explain what each records.
answer: The current account records the net value of transactions in goods and services, primary income and secondary income.
The balance on goods and services is the difference between export and import receipts; the net primary income balance records interest and dividends paid to and received from overseas.
The capital and financial account records transactions in assets, including foreign investment into and out of Australia.
In principle a deficit on the current account is offset by a surplus on the capital and financial account, since the two must sum to zero.

points.title: Free trade agreements
points.detail: Bilateral and multilateral agreements, the trade creation and trade diversion effects, and the impact on Australian industries and living standards.

questions.q: Explain one benefit and one cost of Australia entering a bilateral free trade agreement.
answer: A benefit is improved access to a large overseas market for Australian exporters, raising export revenue, employment and incomes in those industries.
Consumers also gain from cheaper imports from the partner country.
A cost is trade diversion, where trade shifts to the partner country even though a third country is a lower-cost producer, which is allocatively inefficient.

points.title: Foreign investment
points.detail: Foreign direct and portfolio investment, the reasons for investment inflows, and the effects on capacity, growth and the current account.

questions.q: Explain one benefit and one cost of foreign direct investment in Australia.
answer: A benefit is that foreign investment supplements domestic saving and funds capital projects that would otherwise not proceed.
This expands productive capacity, raises productivity through access to new technology and management practice, and creates employment.
A cost is that returns on that investment flow overseas as dividends and interest, adding to the net primary income outflow and widening the current account deficit.
There may also be concerns about foreign control of strategic assets and reduced domestic decision-making power.

points.area: Unit 4: Managing the economy — AoS 1: Aggregate demand policies and domestic economic stability
points.title: Sources of budget revenue
points.detail: Direct taxes including personal income tax and company tax, indirect taxes including GST and excise, and non-tax revenue.

questions.q: Distinguish between direct and indirect taxes and explain why personal income tax is progressive.
answer: A direct tax is levied on the income or wealth of the individual or entity that bears it, such as personal income tax and company tax.
An indirect tax is levied on a transaction and can be passed on to another party, such as the GST and excise duties.
Personal income tax is progressive because the marginal rate rises as income rises, so higher income earners pay a larger proportion of their income in tax.
This reduces inequality in the distribution of income and improves equity.

points.area: Unit 4: Managing the economy — AoS 1: Aggregate demand policies and domestic economic stability
points.title: Budget expenses
points.detail: Government current spending on goods and services, capital spending on infrastructure, and transfer payments, and the different effects of each on aggregate demand.

questions.q: Distinguish between government current spending, capital spending and transfer payments, and state which has the largest immediate effect on aggregate demand.
answer: Current spending is on day-to-day goods and services such as public sector wages; capital spending is on infrastructure such as roads and hospitals.
Transfer payments, such as pensions and unemployment benefits, redistribute income without the government receiving a good or service in return.
Government spending on goods and services has a direct and immediate effect on aggregate demand, whereas transfers affect demand only once recipients spend them, and some is saved.

points.area: Unit 4: Managing the economy — AoS 1: Aggregate demand policies and domestic economic stability
points.title: Budget outcomes and financing
points.detail: Surplus, deficit and balanced outcomes, the difference between cash and underlying outcomes, and how a deficit is financed and a surplus used.

questions.q: Explain what a budget deficit is and describe two ways it may be financed, including the effect of each.
answer: A budget deficit occurs when total budget expenses exceed total budget receipts in a financial year.
It may be financed by borrowing from the private sector through the issue of government bonds, which adds to public debt and interest obligations.
Heavy domestic borrowing may crowd out private investment by placing upward pressure on interest rates.
It may also be financed by borrowing from overseas, which avoids crowding out domestically but adds to the net primary income outflow on the current account.

points.area: Unit 4: Managing the economy — AoS 1: Aggregate demand policies and domestic economic stability
points.title: Automatic and discretionary stabilisers
points.detail: The countercyclical operation of progressive income tax and unemployment benefits, and the distinction from deliberate discretionary policy changes.

questions.q: Explain how automatic stabilisers operate during a downturn and how they differ from discretionary policy.
answer: During a downturn incomes fall, so progressive income tax receipts fall more than proportionately, leaving households with more disposable income than they would otherwise have.
Unemployment benefits rise automatically as more people lose work, supporting their spending.
Both effects expand the budget deficit and cushion the fall in aggregate demand without any government decision being required.
Discretionary policy is a deliberate change to tax rates or spending programs announced by the government, which takes longer to implement but can be targeted.

points.title: Budgetary policy stance
points.detail: Expansionary and contractionary stances judged by the change in the budget outcome rather than by whether it is in deficit or surplus.

questions.q: A budget moves from a deficit of 40 billion to a deficit of 15 billion. Identify the stance and explain your reasoning.
answer: The stance is contractionary, because the deficit has narrowed by 25 billion.
Stance is determined by the change in the budget outcome from one year to the next, not by whether the budget is in deficit or surplus.
A smaller deficit means the budget is injecting less into the economy than previously, so aggregate demand is being dampened relative to the prior year.

points.area: Unit 4: Managing the economy — AoS 1: Aggregate demand policies and domestic economic stability
points.title: Strengths and weaknesses of budgetary policy
points.detail: The ability to target specific sectors, the effects on equity and supply capacity, against implementation lags, political constraints and debt accumulation.

questions.q: Evaluate budgetary policy by explaining one strength and one weakness as a demand management tool.
answer: A strength is that budgetary policy can be targeted at a specific group, region or industry, such as a payment to low income households who are likely to spend it.
It can also address equity directly through the tax and transfer system, which monetary policy cannot do.
A weakness is the implementation lag, since major changes are usually announced in the annual budget and take time to legislate and take effect.
Political constraints also apply, as governments are reluctant to raise taxes or cut spending, which can make contractionary policy difficult to sustain.

points.title: Monetary policy and the cash rate
points.detail: The role of the Reserve Bank of Australia, the setting of the cash rate target, and its independence from government.

questions.q: Explain what the cash rate is and why the RBA's independence from government matters.
answer: The cash rate is the interest rate on overnight loans between financial institutions in the cash market, and the RBA sets a target for it.
Changes in the cash rate flow through to the interest rates banks charge borrowers and pay savers.
Independence matters because the RBA can raise rates to control inflation without the political pressure that would deter an elected government, which makes the inflation target credible.

points.area: Unit 4: Managing the economy — AoS 1: Aggregate demand policies and domestic economic stability
points.title: Transmission mechanisms of monetary policy
points.detail: The savings and investment, cash flow, asset prices and exchange rate channels through which a change in the cash rate affects aggregate demand.

questions.q: Explain three channels through which a cut in the cash rate stimulates aggregate demand.
answer: Cash flow channel: households with variable rate mortgages have lower repayments, leaving more disposable income for consumption.
Savings and investment channel: the return on saving falls and the cost of borrowing falls, encouraging consumption and making more investment projects profitable.
Asset prices channel: lower rates raise share and property prices, and the resulting wealth effect encourages households to spend more.
Exchange rate channel: lower relative interest rates reduce demand for the dollar, causing a depreciation that raises net exports.

points.title: Monetary policy stance
points.detail: Expansionary, contractionary and neutral stances, the concept of the neutral cash rate, and the reading of a stance from RBA decisions.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by a neutral monetary policy stance.
answer: A neutral stance is one in which the cash rate is at the level that neither stimulates nor dampens aggregate demand.
At this rate, growth is expected to proceed at a sustainable pace with inflation within the target band.
A rate below neutral is expansionary and a rate above neutral is contractionary, so the stance is judged relative to the neutral rate rather than by the level of the rate alone.

points.area: Unit 4: Managing the economy — AoS 1: Aggregate demand policies and domestic economic stability
points.title: Strengths and weaknesses of monetary policy
points.detail: Independence, speed of decision and flexibility against blunt sector-wide impact, transmission lags and reduced effectiveness at very low interest rates.

questions.q: Evaluate monetary policy by explaining one strength and two weaknesses.
answer: A strength is that the RBA board meets regularly and can change the cash rate quickly and independently of political considerations, with immediate effect on market rates.
A weakness is that monetary policy is a blunt instrument affecting the whole economy, so it cannot target a particular region or sector in difficulty.
There is also an impact lag of up to 18 months before a change in the cash rate fully affects spending and inflation.
At very low interest rates its effectiveness is reduced, since rates cannot fall much further and confidence rather than the cost of borrowing may be the constraint on spending.

points.title: Policy mix and complementary policy
points.detail: How budgetary and monetary policy work together or against each other, and the circumstances in which one is better suited than the other.

questions.q: Explain why budgetary policy may be preferred to monetary policy during a severe downturn.
answer: In a severe downturn confidence is low, so households and firms may not borrow and spend even when interest rates are very low.
Interest rates may also already be near zero, leaving little room for further stimulus.
Budgetary policy can inject spending directly into the economy through government spending and transfers, which does not rely on private willingness to borrow.
It can also be targeted at the households and industries most affected, making the stimulus more effective per dollar spent.

points.title: Injections, leakages and the circular flow
points.detail: The circular flow of income, the injections of investment, government spending and exports, the leakages of saving, taxation and imports, and the effect of an imbalance.

questions.q: Name the injections and leakages in the circular flow and explain what happens when injections exceed leakages.
answer: Injections are investment, government spending and exports; leakages are saving, taxation and imports.
When injections exceed leakages, more is being added to the flow of income than is being withdrawn.
Aggregate demand rises, so firms increase output and employment and national income expands.
If this continues beyond the economy's productive capacity it generates demand inflation, so the imbalance is sustainable only while spare capacity exists.

points.title: Public debt and crowding out
points.detail: The accumulation of government debt from sustained deficits, the interest burden on future budgets, and the crowding out of private sector investment.

questions.q: Explain the crowding out effect and one further consequence of sustained budget deficits.
answer: Financing a deficit by borrowing from the domestic private sector increases the demand for available funds.
This places upward pressure on interest rates, raising the cost of borrowing for households and businesses.
Some private investment projects become unprofitable and do not proceed, so public spending has partly displaced private spending.
Sustained deficits also accumulate public debt, and the growing interest bill consumes budget revenue that could otherwise fund services or tax cuts.

points.area: Unit 4: Managing the economy — AoS 2: Aggregate supply policies
points.title: The purpose of aggregate supply policies
points.detail: Expanding productive capacity, lowering the costs of production and raising productivity so that growth can occur without inflation.

questions.q: Explain how aggregate supply policies help resolve the trade-off between the goals of low inflation and full employment.
answer: Aggregate supply policies raise productive capacity and lower unit costs of production, shifting aggregate supply to the right.
The economy can then produce more output without the capacity constraints that generate demand inflation.
Lower unit costs also reduce cost inflationary pressure even as employment rises.
This allows both stronger growth and employment and lower inflation at the same time, easing the short-run trade-off.

points.area: Unit 4: Managing the economy — AoS 2: Aggregate supply policies
points.title: Budgetary supply-side measures
points.detail: Spending on education, training, infrastructure and research, and tax measures such as investment incentives that expand capacity rather than demand.

questions.q: Explain how government spending on infrastructure acts as both an aggregate demand and an aggregate supply policy.
answer: In the short term, construction spending is an injection into the economy that directly raises aggregate demand and employment.
In the longer term, better transport and communications infrastructure reduces the time and cost of moving goods and people.
Lower costs of production raise productivity and shift aggregate supply to the right.
The policy therefore stimulates demand now and expands capacity later, which is why infrastructure is often used during downturns.

questions.q: Explain how a targeted skilled migration program acts as an aggregate supply policy.
answer: Skilled migration increases the size and skill level of the labour force, addressing shortages in specific occupations.
Relieving skill shortages reduces upward pressure on wages in those occupations, lowering the cost of production.
Productive capacity expands and aggregate supply shifts to the right, supporting growth with less inflationary pressure.

questions.q: Explain how competition policy improves efficiency and one cost of relying on it.
answer: Competition policy prevents anti-competitive conduct and reduces barriers to entry so that firms face genuine rivals.
Firms must reduce costs and innovate to retain market share, improving productive and dynamic efficiency.
Lower unit costs shift aggregate supply to the right and prices to consumers fall, improving material living standards.
A cost is structural adjustment, as less efficient firms exit and their workers face unemployment until they retrain and relocate.

points.detail: Measures affecting wage determination, workplace flexibility and industry regulation, and their effects on costs, productivity and equity.

questions.q: Explain how labour market policies can improve aggregate supply and one equity concern they raise.
answer: Policies that allow wages to be linked to productivity at the enterprise level mean wage growth does not outpace output growth, containing unit labour costs.
Greater flexibility in working arrangements can raise participation and allow firms to match labour to demand, improving productivity.
Aggregate supply shifts right, supporting growth with lower inflationary pressure.
An equity concern is that increased flexibility may reduce job security and bargaining power for low-skilled workers, widening income inequality.

points.title: Environmental and energy policies
points.detail: Policies addressing emissions and energy costs, and the tension between short-run costs of production and long-run intertemporal efficiency.

questions.q: Explain the short-run and long-run effects of a policy subsidising renewable energy investment on aggregate supply.
answer: In the short run the subsidy is a budget cost, and the transition may raise energy costs for some producers, restraining aggregate supply.
In the long run, cheaper and more reliable energy lowers a significant input cost across the economy.
This raises productivity and shifts aggregate supply to the right, supporting non-inflationary growth.
It also improves intertemporal efficiency by reducing the environmental costs imposed on future generations, supporting non-material living standards.

points.area: Unit 4: Managing the economy — AoS 2: Aggregate supply policies
points.title: Evaluating supply-side policies
points.detail: The long implementation and impact lags, budgetary costs and distributional effects of supply-side measures, compared with demand-side policy.

questions.q: Explain two limitations of relying on aggregate supply policies to manage the economy.
answer: Supply-side policies have very long impact lags; education and infrastructure investment may take a decade to raise productive capacity measurably.
They are therefore poorly suited to stabilising the economy over the business cycle, where a rapid response is needed.
Many involve substantial budgetary cost, which worsens the budget outcome and adds to public debt in the short term.
Some, such as deregulation, produce structural unemployment and widen inequality, so they carry political and equity costs.

points.area: Unit 4: Managing the economy — AoS 2: Aggregate supply policies
points.title: Equity and the distribution of income
points.detail: The distinction between efficiency and equity, the effect of the tax and transfer system on the distribution of income, and the trade-offs policy makers face.

questions.q: Explain the potential trade-off between efficiency and equity using an example from tax policy.
answer: Efficiency concerns the allocation and productive use of resources, while equity concerns the fairness of the distribution of income.
A highly progressive income tax improves equity by redistributing income from higher to lower income earners.
However, high marginal rates may reduce the incentive to work additional hours, invest or take entrepreneurial risk, which reduces efficiency and productive capacity.
Policy makers must therefore balance the equity gains from redistribution against the efficiency cost of reduced incentives.

points.area: Exam technique and data analysis
points.title: Interpreting economic data
points.detail: Reading tables and graphs of GDP growth, inflation, unemployment and the exchange rate, describing trends accurately and quoting figures with units and periods.

questions.q: State three features of a strong description of a trend in economic data.
answer: State the direction of the change and whether it accelerated, slowed or reversed over the period.
Quote specific figures with their units and the periods to which they relate, including the start and end values.
Identify any turning point or anomaly rather than describing only the overall movement.

points.area: Exam technique and data analysis
points.title: Building an economic chain of reasoning
points.detail: Linking a cause to an effect through each intermediate step, and connecting the final step back to a macroeconomic goal or to living standards.

questions.q: Explain what a complete chain of reasoning looks like in an Economics response and why missing links cost marks.
answer: Begin with the cause, then state each step in sequence: the effect on a component of aggregate demand or supply, then on the relevant economic variable.
Then state the effect on the macroeconomic goal, and finally on material or non-material living standards.
Marks are awarded for the links, not just the conclusion, so skipping from cause straight to outcome loses the intermediate marks.
Each step should state the direction of change and the mechanism that produces it.

points.area: Exam technique and data analysis
points.title: Command terms and mark allocation
points.detail: The depth required by identify, describe, explain, analyse, discuss and evaluate, and matching the number of distinct points to the marks available.

questions.q: Explain how the mark allocation should guide the structure of an Economics response.
answer: The number of marks indicates roughly how many distinct linked points are required, so a four-mark explanation needs about four developed links.
Command terms determine the depth: describe requires an account, explain requires reasons and mechanism, and evaluate requires both sides plus a judgement.
Check whether the question asks about one effect or two, and whether it specifies a particular goal or policy, and address exactly what is asked.
